data.about: The same 16 by 12 metre slab as task 2, but the walls have moved: one up each side and one along the top, and now the force is 100 kN and the answer has to be a number. Three walls, three unknowns, three equations — the slab is statically determinate in plan, which is why graphic statics on the wall centrelines and a stiffness distribution give the same answer here. Then the pretty part: the resultant of the load and the first wall reaction happens to point exactly at the corner where the other two wall axes cross, so a single straight strut across the slab does the entire job. The force diagram is a rectangle and the strut is its diagonal.

data.text: form diagrams 1:100 — a vertical over the roller, a diagonal to the pin

steps.caption: EX 10 task 3: the same slab, the walls moved, and now a number. F = 100 kN comes in at the left edge and has to end up in the ground through three walls. Find the flow, find the force in every member, and draw the force diagram at 1 cm ≙ 10 kN
steps.title: The exercise

steps.caption: a 16 by 12 metre slab at 1:200. Wall A runs up the left edge, wall C up the right edge, wall B along the top on the right-hand half. All three are 5.00 by 0.40 metres, and not one dimension is printed on the sheet — everything here is measured off the drawing against its stated scale
steps.title: The plan

steps.caption: each centreline run right across the plan. A wall only absorbs force along its own axis, so A and C can take y and B can take x — three unknown magnitudes on three known lines, against the three equilibrium equations of a body in plane. The slab is statically determinate: this is plain statics, and a stiffness-based sharing would return the identical numbers
steps.title: Three axes, three unknowns

steps.caption: axes A and C are parallel; axis B crosses both. Two distinct crossings, so by the compendium's own test the slab is properly braced — and the second of them, at the top right, is where the whole solution is going to happen
steps.title: Braced

steps.caption: F = 100 kN enters at (0.00, 6.00) and its line of action runs across the slab. Where it meets wall A's axis is the node N₁ — the one place the load and one wall can be added together
steps.title: The load, and the first node

steps.caption: add F and wall A's reaction at N₁ and the resultant is (100.0, 37.18) kN. Follow that line across the slab and at x = 15.80 it has climbed to exactly y = 11.80 — the corner N₂ where wall B's axis crosses wall C's. Nothing was arranged to make that happen; it is what the three equilibrium equations already decided
steps.title: One strut, and it aims itself

steps.caption: the strut arrives at N₂ carrying both components. The horizontal 100 kN goes straight into wall B, because N₂ actually lies on wall B. The vertical 37.18 kN runs down wall C's axis as a tie. And back at N₁, the short link down to wall A is a strut, because wall A has to push the node up
steps.title: Resolve at the far corner

steps.caption: at 1 cm ≙ 10 kN. The four external forces close a RECTANGLE — F along the bottom, A up the right side, B back along the top, C down the left — and the strut is its diagonal. Measure it: 10.669 cm, and it really is drawn longer than the 16 m slab is wide, because the slab is at 1:200 and this is not
steps.title: The force diagram

steps.caption: F and wall B are a pair of equal, opposite, offset forces — a couple. Walls A and C are the couple that cancels it. Two completely different levers, one number, and if they did not agree the drawing would be wrong
steps.title: The couple, checked both ways

steps.caption: the little solid triangle beside each wall says which way you look at it, and the elevation's right-hand direction is that view direction crossed with up. Walls A and C are both seen along +x, so both put the slab's bottom edge at the elevation's right and both take their load at the LEFT end — A pushing right, C pushing left, which is exactly what makes them a couple. Only the pin can take H, so the diagonal always runs to the pin
steps.title: Each wall, unfolded

steps.caption: A = C = 37.18 kN and B = 100.00 kN, carried across the slab by one 106.69 kN strut at 20.39°. Drag y_F to 11.80 and A and C vanish — the load walks straight into wall B; drag wall C towards wall A and the lever arm collapses and the reactions blow up
steps.title: The answer

data.title: EX 10.3 — one strut carries the whole slab
